name: Chapter 5: Work, Energy and Power
description: Dot product, work, kinetic energy, work-energy theorem, potential energy, springs, conservation of energy, power, collisions

cards.term: Define the scalar (dot) product.
cards.definition: \[\vec A \cdot \vec B = AB\cos\theta\]a scalar, θ = angle between the vectors

cards.term: Geometric meaning of A · B?
cards.definition: |A| × (component of B along A) = |B| × (projection of A on B)

cards.text: The dot product is {{c1::commutative}} (A·B = B·A) and {{c2::distributive}} (A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C).

cards.term: î·î and î·ĵ?
cards.definition: î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1; î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0

cards.term: A · B in components?
cards.definition: \[A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z\]

cards.term: What does A · B = 0 mean (non-zero vectors)?
cards.definition: A and B are perpendicular

cards.term: A · A = ?
Example 5.1: F = 3î + 4ĵ − 5k̂, d = 5î + 4ĵ + 3k̂. Angle between them?
Teacher addition: projection of A on B?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{\vec A \cdot \vec B}{|\vec B|}\]

cards.term: How does v² − u² = 2as lead to the work-energy idea?
cards.definition: Multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs

cards.term: State the work-energy theorem.
cards.definition: Change in kinetic energy of a particle = work done on it by the net force: K𝒻 − Kᵢ = W

cards.term: Correction: NCERT 5.2 says v² − u² = 2as was met "in Chapter 3". Where was it?
cards.definition: In Chapter 2 (Motion in a Straight Line); the reference is left over from the old numbering

cards.term: Raindrop: work by air resistance
cards.definition: W(resistive) = ΔK − W(gravity) = 1.25 − 10 = −8.75 J

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 5.2 · raindrop

Find the missing step.

1.00 g drop falls 1.00 km and hits the ground at 50.0 m/s (g = 10). Work by the resistive force?
  1. ΔK = ½ × 10⁻³ × 50² = 1.25 J
  2. W(gravity) = mgh = 10⁻³ × 10 × 10³ = 10.0 J
  3. ?
  4. W(resistive) = 1.25 − 10 = −8.75 J
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 5.2 · raindrop

Find the missing step.

1.00 g drop falls 1.00 km and hits the ground at 50.0 m/s (g = 10). Work by the resistive force?
  1. ΔK = ½ × 10⁻³ × 50² = 1.25 J
  2. W(gravity) = mgh = 10⁻³ × 10 × 10³ = 10.0 J
  3. W-E theorem: ΔK = W(gravity) + W(resistive)
  4. W(resistive) = 1.25 − 10 = −8.75 J

cards.term: What does Example 5.2 show about unknown forces?
cards.definition: The work of a force can be found from the W-E theorem without knowing the force law

cards.term: Define work done by a constant force.
cards.definition: \[W = Fd\cos\theta = \vec F \cdot \vec d\]component of force along the displacement × displacement

cards.term: When is no work done?
cards.definition: Pushing a rigid wall: displacement = 0; Weightlifter holding 150 kg steady: displacement = 0; Block sliding on a smooth table (horizontal): horizontal force = 0; Gravity on a block moving horizontally: F ⟂ d; Earth’s pull on the Moon (circular orbit): F ⟂ d

cards.term: Why do you get tired pushing a wall though no work is done on it?
cards.definition: Your muscles repeatedly contract and relax, using internal energy

cards.term: Sign of work for θ < 90°, θ = 90°, θ > 90°?
cards.definition: Positive, zero, negative (friction usually has θ = 180°)

cards.term: Dimensions and SI unit of work and energy?
cards.definition: [M L² T⁻²]; joule (J), after James Prescott Joule

cards.term: Alternative units of work and energy (Table 5.1)
cards.definition: 1 erg: 10⁻⁷ J; 1 electron volt (eV): 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; 1 calorie (cal): 4.186 J; 1 kilowatt hour (kWh): 3.6 × 10⁶ J

cards.term: Example 5.3: a cyclist skids to a stop in 10 m; road force 200 N. Work by the road on the cycle, and by the cycle on the road?
cards.definition: −2000 J on the cycle; zero on the road (the road does not move)

cards.term: Lesson of Example 5.3?
cards.definition: Action and reaction are equal and opposite, but the work they do need not be equal and opposite

cards.term: Signs of work (Exercise 5.1)
cards.definition: Man lifting a bucket out of a well: positive; Gravity on that bucket: negative; Friction on a body sliding down an incline: negative; Applied force, body moving uniformly on rough floor: positive; Air resistance on a swinging pendulum: negative

cards.term: Exercise 5.11: F = (−î + 2ĵ + 3k̂) N; the body moves 4 m along z. Work?
cards.definition: Only the z-component works: 3 × 4 = 12 J

cards.term: Kinetic energy formula; scalar or vector?
cards.definition: \[K = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 m\,\vec v \cdot \vec v\]a scalar, never negative

cards.term: Relation between kinetic energy and momentum?
cards.definition: \[K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}, \quad p = \sqrt{2mK}\]

cards.term: Same kinetic energy: which has more momentum, a heavy or a light body?
cards.definition: The heavier (p = √(2mK))

cards.term: Same momentum: which has more kinetic energy?
cards.definition: The lighter (K = p²/2m)

cards.term: Table 5.2: typical kinetic energies of a car, a bullet, an air molecule?
cards.definition: Car ~6 × 10⁵ J, bullet ~10³ J, air molecule ~10⁻²¹ J

cards.term: Example 5.4: 50 g bullet at 200 m/s keeps 10 % of its KE after passing through plywood. Emergent speed?
cards.definition: 63.2 m/s: speed falls by about 68 %, not 90 % (K ∝ v²)

cards.term: Exercise 5.12: electron with 10 keV, proton with 100 keV. Which is faster?
cards.definition: The electron, about 13.5× faster (v = √(2K/m))

cards.term: Work done by a variable force?
cards.definition: \[W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx\]= area under the F–x graph

cards.term: Area below the x-axis on an F–x graph?
cards.definition: Negative work (force opposite to displacement)

cards.term: Example 5.5: a woman pushes a trunk with 100 N for 10 m, then her force falls linearly to 50 N at 20 m; friction is 50 N. Work by each?
cards.definition: Woman: 1000 + 750 = 1750 J; friction: −1000 J

cards.term: Proof of the W-E theorem for a variable force?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{dK}{dt} = mv\dfrac{dv}{dt} = Fv = F\dfrac{dx}{dt} \Rightarrow dK = F\,dx\]then integrate

cards.term: W-E theorem vs Newton’s second law: what information is lost?
cards.definition: It is a scalar, integrated form: the time and direction information of F = ma is not available

cards.term: Example 5.6: 1 kg block at 2 m/s crosses a patch with F = −k/x (k = 0.5 J) from 0.1 m to 2.01 m. Final speed?
cards.definition: K𝒻 = 2 − 0.5 ln(20.1) = 2 − 1.5 = 0.5 J → v = 1 m/s

cards.term: Exercise 5.20: 0.5 kg body moves with v = a x^(3/2), a = 5 m^(−1/2) s⁻¹. Work by the net force from x = 0 to 2 m?
cards.definition: v² at x = 2 is 25 × 8 = 200, so W = ΔK = ½ × 0.5 × 200 = 50 J

cards.term: Exercise 5.2: 2 kg body pulled by 7 N on a table, μₖ = 0.1, for 10 s. Work by F, friction, net force?
cards.definition: 882 J, −247 J, 635 J = ΔK (W-E theorem)

cards.term: What is potential energy?
cards.definition: "Stored" energy due to the position or configuration of a body (stretched bowstring, strained fault lines)

cards.term: Gravitational PE near Earth’s surface?
cards.definition: \( V(h) = mgh \) (for h ≪ R, g constant), with V = 0 at the ground

cards.term: Relation between a conservative force and its potential energy (1D)?
cards.definition: \[F(x) = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}\]ΔV = −(work done by the force)

cards.term: Why the minus sign in F = −dV/dx?
cards.definition: The force points towards decreasing potential energy (gravity pulls down as V = mgh grows upward)

cards.term: Block slides from rest down a smooth incline of height h. Speed at the bottom?
cards.definition: \( \sqrt{2gh} \), independent of the angle (gravity is conservative)

cards.term: Is potential energy defined for friction?
cards.definition: No: friction is non-conservative; its work depends on the path

cards.term: State the conservation of mechanical energy.
cards.definition: If only conservative forces do work, K + V stays constant

cards.term: Definitions of a conservative force
cards.definition: 1: F = −dV/dx for some scalar V(x); 2: Work depends only on the end points; 3: Work over any closed path is zero

cards.term: Ball dropped from height H: speed at height h?
cards.definition: \( v = \sqrt{2g(H - h)} \); at the ground, \( \sqrt{2gH} \)

cards.term: Example 5.7: a bob just completes a vertical circle (string slack only at the top). v at A (bottom), B (side), C (top)?
cards.definition: \[\sqrt{5gL},\ \sqrt{3gL},\ \sqrt{gL}\]

cards.term: Why is v = √(gL) at the top of the vertical circle?
cards.definition: Tension is zero there, so gravity alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/L

cards.term: Example 5.7: ratio of kinetic energies at B and C?
cards.definition: 3 : 1

cards.term: Example 5.7: what happens if the string is cut at C?
cards.definition: The bob has horizontal velocity √(gL) → a projectile path, like a stone kicked off a cliff

cards.term: Why does tension do no work on a pendulum bob?
cards.definition: Tension is always perpendicular to the bob’s displacement

cards.term: Is the zero of potential energy fixed?
cards.definition: No: it is arbitrary, but once chosen it must be kept throughout the problem

cards.term: Energy with a non-conservative force?
cards.definition: \[E_f - E_i = W_{nc}\]change in mechanical energy = work by non-conservative forces (path dependent)

cards.term: Exercise 5.18: bob released from horizontal, L = 1.5 m, loses 5 % of its energy. Speed at the bottom?
cards.definition: 5.3 m/s (½v² = 0.95 gL)

cards.term: Hooke’s law and unit of k?
cards.definition: \( F_s = -kx \); k in N m⁻¹. Stiff spring: large k

cards.term: Work done by the spring force when it is stretched by xₘ from its natural length?
cards.definition: \[W_s = -\tfrac12 kx_m^2\](triangle under the Fₛ–x line); the pulling force does +½kxₘ²

cards.term: Work done by the spring force from xᵢ to x𝒻?
cards.definition: \[W_s = -\tfrac12 k(x_f^2 - x_i^2)\]zero over a closed cycle → conservative

cards.term: Potential energy of a spring?
cards.definition: \[V(x) = \tfrac12 kx^2\]zero at the natural length

cards.term: Spring–block: KE and PE exchange, total constant
cards.definition: At the ends all PE and v = 0; at x = 0 all KE and v max = A√(k/m); K + V = ½kA² constant

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Spring · energy exchange

A block on a smooth floor oscillates on a spring between −A and +A. How do its KE and PE change, and where is it fastest?

Picture two bars, KE and PE.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Spring · energy exchange

A block on a smooth floor oscillates on a spring between −A and +A. How do its KE and PE change, and where is it fastest?

At ±A: all PE (½kA²), v = 0. At x = 0: all KE, speed maximum v = A√(k/m).

K + V = ½kA² stays constant: the two parabolas of Fig. 5.8 are mirror images.

cards.term: Block on a spring released from xₘ: maximum speed, and where?
cards.definition: \[v_m = x_m\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}\]at the equilibrium position x = 0

cards.term: Exercise 5.4: V = ½kx², k = 0.5 N/m, total energy 1 J. Where does the particle turn back?
cards.definition: Where V = E: ½ × 0.5 × x² = 1 → x = ±2 m (KE would be negative beyond)

cards.term: Example 5.8 (NCERT): a 1000 kg car at 18 km/h hits a spring, k = 5.25 × 10³ N/m. NCERT’s maximum compression?
cards.definition: 2.00 m (½mv² = ½kxₘ², K = 1.25 × 10⁴ J)

cards.term: Correction: recompute Example 5.8 with k = 5.25 × 10³ N/m as printed.
cards.definition: xₘ = √(2 × 12500 / 5250) = 2.18 m. NCERT’s 2.00 m (and 1.35 m in Example 5.9) fit k = 6.25 × 10³ N/m; the printed k is a typo

cards.term: Example 5.9: the same car with friction μ = 0.5. Equation for xₘ?
cards.definition: \[\tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 kx_m^2 + \mu mg\,x_m\]→ with k = 6.25 × 10³: 1.35 m (less than without friction)

cards.term: Useful conversion from Example 5.8?
cards.definition: 36 km/h = 10 m/s (multiply km/h by 5/18)

cards.term: What can energy conservation NOT tell you in the car–spring problem?
cards.definition: The time taken to compress; that needs Newton’s second law

cards.term: Define average and instantaneous power.
cards.definition: \[P_{av} = \dfrac{W}{t},\quad P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \vec F \cdot \vec v\]

cards.term: Unit and dimensions of power; 1 hp?
cards.definition: watt (1 W = 1 J/s), [M L² T⁻³]; 1 hp = 746 W

cards.term: Is kWh a unit of power?
cards.definition: No: of energy. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (a 100 W bulb for 10 h)

cards.term: Elevator motor power

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 5.10 · elevator

Find the missing step.

1800 kg elevator rises at a constant 2 m/s against 4000 N friction (g = 10). Minimum motor power?
  1. Constant speed → motor force balances the downward forces
  2. ?
  3. P = Fv = 22000 × 2 = 44000 W
  4. = 44000 / 746 ≈ 59 hp
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 5.10 · elevator

Find the missing step.

1800 kg elevator rises at a constant 2 m/s against 4000 N friction (g = 10). Minimum motor power?
  1. Constant speed → motor force balances the downward forces
  2. F = mg + f = 18000 + 4000 = 22000 N
  3. P = Fv = 22000 × 2 = 44000 W
  4. = 44000 / 746 ≈ 59 hp

cards.term: Exercise 5.9: body from rest with constant acceleration. Power delivered ∝ ?
cards.definition: t (P = Fv = ma · at)

cards.term: Exercise 5.10: body driven by a constant power. Displacement ∝ ?
cards.definition: t^(3/2) (½mv² = Pt → v ∝ t^½)

cards.term: Exercise 5.15: a pump fills 30 m³ at 40 m height in 15 min with 30 % efficiency. Electric power?
cards.definition: Useful power = 30000 × 9.8 × 40 / 900 ≈ 13.1 kW → input 43.6 kW

cards.term: Exercise 5.21: windmill of area A, wind speed v, air density ρ. Mass and KE of the air in time t?
cards.definition: \[m = \rho A v t,\quad K = \tfrac12 \rho A v^3 t\]25 % of that with A = 30 m², v = 10 m/s → 4.5 kW

cards.term: What is conserved in every collision?
cards.definition: Total linear momentum (and total energy); kinetic energy only in elastic collisions

cards.term: Why is momentum conserved in a collision whatever the forces?
cards.definition: By the third law, the impulses on the two bodies are equal and opposite at every instant

cards.term: Elastic, inelastic and completely inelastic collisions
cards.definition: Elastic: conserved; Inelastic: partly lost (heat, sound, deformation); Completely inelastic: maximum loss; bodies move together

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
5.11.1 · types of collision

Kinetic energy after the collision?

Elastic?
Inelastic?
Completely inelastic?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
5.11.1 · types of collision

Kinetic energy after the collision?

Elasticconserved
Inelasticpartly lost (heat, sound, deformation)
Completely inelasticmaximum loss; bodies move together

cards.term: During an elastic collision (balls in contact), is KE conserved?
cards.definition: No: KE is conserved only after the collision; during contact some is stored as deformation. Momentum is conserved at every instant

cards.term: Completely inelastic collision: m₁ at v hits m₂ at rest. Common velocity?
KE lost in that completely inelastic collision?
cards.definition: \[\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v^2\]

cards.term: Elastic 1D collision, m₂ at rest: final velocities?
Elastic 1D collision: relative velocity before and after?
cards.definition: Speed of separation = speed of approach:\[v_{2f} - v_{1f} = v_{1i} - v_{2i}\](coefficient of restitution e = 1)

cards.term: Equal masses: elastic exchange vs sticking together
cards.definition: Elastic: A stops, B moves at v. Completely inelastic: both at v/2, half the KE lost

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Collisions · 1D

Ball A (speed v) hits an identical ball B at rest. What happens if the collision is elastic? If they stick together?

Momentum is conserved in both.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Collisions · 1D

Ball A (speed v) hits an identical ball B at rest. What happens if the collision is elastic? If they stick together?

Elastic: velocities exchange — A stops, B moves off with v. KE and momentum both conserved.

Completely inelastic: common velocity v/2 (momentum mv = 2m·v/2); half the KE is lost as heat and sound.

cards.term: Special cases of elastic collisions
cards.definition: m₁ = m₂: m₁ stops, m₂ moves off with v₁ᵢ (velocities exchange); m₂ ≫ m₁ (ball on a wall): m₁ bounces back with −v₁ᵢ; m₂ stays at rest; m₁ ≫ m₂: m₁ barely slows; m₂ flies off at ≈ 2v₁ᵢ

Result?

m₁ = m₂?
m₂ ≫ m₁ (ball on a wall)?
m₁ ≫ m₂?

m₁ ≫ m₂m₁ barely slows; m₂ flies off at ≈ 2v₁ᵢ

cards.term: Example 5.11: why are heavy water or graphite used as moderators?
cards.definition: A neutron loses most of its KE to a light nucleus: deuterium takes 8/9 of it per head-on collision, carbon 28.4 %

cards.term: Fraction of KE a neutron keeps after a head-on elastic collision with a nucleus of mass m₂?
cards.definition: \[f_1 = \left(\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)^2\]deuterium: 1/9, carbon: 71.6 %

cards.term: What is a head-on (1D) collision?
cards.definition: Initial and final velocities lie on one line: the path of body 1 passes through the centre of body 2

cards.term: 2D collision, m₂ at rest: momentum equations?
cards.definition: \[m_1v_{1i} = m_1v_{1f}\cos\theta_1 + m_2v_{2f}\cos\theta_2;\ \ 0 = m_1v_{1f}\sin\theta_1 - m_2v_{2f}\sin\theta_2\]

cards.term: Why can a 2D elastic collision not be solved from the conservation laws alone?
cards.definition: Four unknowns (two final speeds, two angles) but only three equations; one (e.g. θ₁) must be measured

cards.term: Example 5.12: equal billiard balls, elastic glancing collision, target goes off at 37°. Angle of the cue ball?
cards.definition: 53°: equal masses, one at rest → they move off at 90° to each other

cards.term: What is scattering?
cards.definition: A "collision" through action at a distance without touching (a comet near the Sun, an α-particle near a nucleus)

cards.term: Exercise 5.16: a ball hits two identical touching balls head-on (elastic). Result?
cards.definition: The first two end at rest; the last ball moves off with V

cards.term: Exercise 5.17: bob A released from 30° hits identical bob B at rest (elastic). How high does A rise?
cards.definition: Not at all: equal masses exchange velocities; A stops and B moves on

cards.term: Exercise 5.19: sand leaks out of a trolley moving at 27 km/h on a frictionless track. Final speed?
cards.definition: 27 km/h: the sand leaves with the trolley’s own velocity, so no horizontal force acts

cards.term: Exercise 5.14: a molecule hits a wall at 200 m/s, 30° to the normal, and rebounds with the same speed. Momentum conserved? Elastic?
cards.definition: Momentum of molecule + wall is conserved (the wall’s recoil is negligible); KE is conserved → elastic

cards.term: Exercise 5.5(b): why is the work done by the Sun’s gravity on a comet zero over each full orbit?
cards.definition: Gravity is conservative; over a closed path the PE returns to its starting value

cards.term: Exercise 5.5(c): a satellite loses energy to air drag, yet it speeds up as it spirals in. Why?
cards.definition: PE falls twice as fast as the total energy, so KE rises (for a circular orbit KE = −E)

cards.term: Exercise 5.5(a): the casing of a rocket burns up by friction. Whose energy is used?
cards.definition: The rocket’s (its kinetic and potential energy)

cards.term: Exercise 5.5(d): a man walks 2 m carrying 15 kg in his hands, or walks 2 m pulling a rope that lifts 15 kg over a pulley. When is more work done?
cards.definition: Pulling: the load rises, W = mgh = 15 × 9.8 × 2 = 294 J. Carrying horizontally does no work against gravity

cards.term: Energy concept checks (Exercises 5.6–5.7)
cards.definition: Conservative force does positive work → PE…: decreases; Work against friction costs…: kinetic energy; Inelastic collision: unchanged quantities: total momentum and total energy; Work over a closed loop is zero for every force: False (friction); Inelastic collision: final KE < initial KE, always: False (usually, not always)

cards.term: Exercise 5.3 (Fig. 5.11): with total energy E, where can a particle NOT be found?
cards.definition: Where V(x) > E (KE would be negative). The minimum energy needed is the lowest V

cards.term: Exercise 5.22: lifting 10 kg through 0.5 m, 1000 times. Work against gravity, and fat used at 20 % efficiency (3.8 × 10⁷ J/kg)?
cards.definition: 49 000 J and 6.45 × 10⁻³ kg
